1054954,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.4.1.2,1935-03-07,e885929f-c4c1-4965-b723-ad4350f8b072,ca.m.5276,Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Immigration) :,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines,BRITISH SETTLERS,REPORTED DISTRESS OF IMMIGRANTS UNDER THREE THOUSAND BRITISH FAMILIES SCHEME IN NORTHERN SASKATCHEWAN,,I wish to answer an inquiry that was made yesterday by the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) with respect to certain newspaper reports having to do with a number of settlers under what is known as the three thousand British families scheme.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Wesley Ashton Gordon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e885929f-c4c1-4965-b723-ad4350f8b072&Language=E&Section=ALL
1054955,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.4.1.3,1935-03-07,7ae29289-fb11-4e01-becc-dd3d1aa8a695,ca.m.8203,Mr. VALLANCE:,,BRITISH SETTLERS,REPORTED DISTRESS OF IMMIGRANTS UNDER THREE THOUSAND BRITISH FAMILIES SCHEME IN NORTHERN SASKATCHEWAN,,May I correct the minister? These are not newspaper reports; they were reports made to me direct.

,Liberal,,John Vallance,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=7ae29289-fb11-4e01-becc-dd3d1aa8a695&Language=E&Section=ALL
1054956,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.4.1.4,1935-03-07,e885929f-c4c1-4965-b723-ad4350f8b072,ca.m.5276,Mr. GORDON:,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines,BRITISH SETTLERS,REPORTED DISTRESS OF IMMIGRANTS UNDER THREE THOUSAND BRITISH FAMILIES SCHEME IN NORTHERN SASKATCHEWAN,,Whether they were newspaper reports or not, I will try to answer the question. I have had inquiries made and it would appear that these settlers came to Canada under an empire agreement with the British government about ben years ago. A great numlber of t)he settlers have done very well, and some of them not so well.
On January 28 last a delegation of these settlers called at the office of the chief field
British Settlers

supervisor at Prinice Albert. There were nine families represented. I do not think it would be fair to name the families, but the spokesman for the delegation stated that the families had been induced to emigrate on promises which were not fulfilled and that the settlers required relief in food and clothing. Then they submitted what was almost an ultimatum, as follows:
(a) The group of settlers must be repatriated to the United Kingdom.
(lb) Allowances must be provided by the dominion government to keep the families in reasonable comfort until repatriation was carried out.

column2: The settlers would not operate their farms this spring.

If allowances made by the dominion government were considered insufficient, application would be made to the British government for authority to dispose of stock and equipment purchased out of British funds; and
A reply must be made within a period of two weeks.

column1: A report was immediately submitted by the district superintendent at Saskatoon and on the 9th ultimo the district superintendent was advised that on checking over the records here it was found that these families had come to Canada between 1926 and 1929 and had already acquired Canadian domicile by five years' residence. Therefore we have no machinery that can be put in motion to return these families to Britain.

The attention of the district superintendent was also directed to the fact that the distribution of relief is not in the hands of this department and that these families would be entitled to the same treatment as other residents whether born in Canada or abroad, and further that the settlers would have the same rights as other farmers under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act for a readjustment of indebtedness. One of the settlers, Mr. Fraser, acted as spokesman. He wired to the director on the thirteenth ultimo refusing to accept the department's reply to the delegation's demands and said that they would remain in occupancy of the Prince Albert office until the director would interview them personally.

On Thursday the fourteenth ultimo, the district superintendent at Saskatoon was instructed by long distance telephone to offer to transport the settlers back to their farms and to advise them that if any difficulty was met with in obtaining relief, he, the district superintendent, would take the matter up with the proper authorities. As is well known, the dominion government, acting in conjunction with the government of the province, is making

provision for necessitous cases throughout the whole province. The district superintendent was told to advise the delegation that the office was to be closed at the usual closing hour in the evening and they would be removed unless they left the premises.

Reports to hand show that the land settlement officer offered to provide transportation for any who wanted it. Two of the families who lived fourteen and nine miles respectively from Prince Albert had driven to the city in their own automobiles bringing some of the others with them. None of the delegates accepted the offer of transportation. They left the office shortly after three o'clock in the afternoon of the fourteenth without any force or persuasion beyond the advice of the land settlement officer. A press report of the fifteenth ultimo stated that the remnant of the delegation started to walk home distances of from ten to fifteen miles and that there were some women in the group. As there was only one woman who appeared at the land settlement office after the first day and as she and her husband drove their own automobile, the press report is evidently incorrect.

Then the director wrote to the spokesman for the group setting out the position of the department in the matter. It is quite obvious that these people, having resided in Canada as long as they have, while they may have_ met with difficulties, have assumed an attitude which in my judgment is at least not well considered, and if they find themselves at the moment in need of assistance, there is a proper source, namely the provincial authorities, who undoubtedly can take care of their situation.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Wesley Ashton Gordon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e885929f-c4c1-4965-b723-ad4350f8b072&Language=E&Section=ALL

,,,Some hon. MEMBERS:,
1054967,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.5.1.9,1935-03-07,48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97,ca.m.2450,Mr. MITCHELL:,,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION,,Why six months? That seems like too long a period in which to make the choice of a commissioner. I see no reason why the government of the day could not choose a man within twenty-eight days. The amendment means in effect that two commissioners can sit for six months and adjudicate on problems coming before the commission without the advice, it may be of the labour representative, who is in ill health or dead, or it may be of the representative of the manufacturers, or it may be of a man of judicial qualification who is the chairman.

I see no reason why six months should be necessary, and I would like the government to take into consideration shortening that period to at least twenty-eight days. That is ample time for making a decision in regard to an appointment.

,Labour,,Humphrey Mitchell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97&Language=E&Section=ALL
1054968,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.5.1.10,1935-03-07,4430053b-1f47-481d-9354-7a7535f63be9,ca.m.8546,Sir GEORGE PERLEY:,Minister Without Portfolio,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION,,The hon. gentleman must not imagine that any government would have the intention of taking the full six months, but there are times of the year

column2: when for various reasons it is difficult to *make these arrangements. In some parts of
the year it is easy, but at other times there F is a good deal of difficulty because of the

column1: holiday season and one thing or another. I think my hon. friend may rely on any government, even if it be one of his own way of thinking, to make a decision without taking the full six months.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,George Halsey Perley,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4430053b-1f47-481d-9354-7a7535f63be9&Language=E&Section=ALL
1054969,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.5.1.11,1935-03-07,bec983fd-5d93-4fb8-b921-3a1d702cbebd,ca.m.3148,Mr. GARLAND (Bow River):,,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION,,I feel

quite sympathetic toward the position taken just now by the acting Prime Minister, but I still think six months is too long a period. I agree with him that twenty-eight days might be hardly enough, and I would suggest that three months, as the period during which the appointment would be expected to take place, would be ample, taking into consideration almost all factors that could be anticipated. I think three months would be fair under the circumstances.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,Edward Joseph Garland,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=bec983fd-5d93-4fb8-b921-3a1d702cbebd&Language=E&Section=ALL
1054970,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.5.1.12,1935-03-07,4430053b-1f47-481d-9354-7a7535f63be9,ca.m.8546,Sir GEORGE PERLEY:,Minister Without Portfolio,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION,,I am within the good sense of the committee on this subject. To my mind it does not make a great deal of difference, because such an officer would be very necessary and I think any government would make this appointment as soon as possible. But I want to submit to my hon. friends that there is a time of the year when for two months or more in the holiday season very few people and sometimes very few members of the government are here. I will compromise on four months. I have had a good deal of experience of holidays in that connection. When ministers are away attending to their duties in various parts of the country, it is sometimes difficult to decide on a first class man to fill one of these important positions.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,George Halsey Perley,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4430053b-1f47-481d-9354-7a7535f63be9&Language=E&Section=ALL
1054971,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.5.1.13,1935-03-07,48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97,ca.m.2450,Mr. MITCHELL:,,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION,,Might I make this suggestion, which I think is practical? Reducing the time would at least shorten the agony for the government. I am not unmindful of the large numbers who would probably offer themselves for a position of this description, and I think from a purely practical point of view a decision made quickly would probably be just as sound as if the government waited a full six months, or four, as the case might be. The number of men in the dominion who in my judgment could ably fill this position is not large, and in the interest of smooth administration I suggest that the shortest period of time should be stipulated in which a vacancy occurring in the commission should be filled. We have heard recently in the house of the office of a deputy minister being vacant for four or five years; and such a thing might occur in connection with this commission. We of the labour movement are anxious that when
Unemployment Insuranc'e
these vacancies occur, particularly if it is a Wbour vacancy, it should be filled at the earliest possible moment.

,Labour,,Humphrey Mitchell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97&Language=E&Section=ALL

1054975,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.5.1.17,1935-03-07,17232084-6a45-4ebd-bd5d-cab516ff3bfd,ca.m.691,Mr. BRADETTE:,,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION,,When I spoke previously on this matter I believe I was misunderstood by the Prime Minister. 1055020,ca.proc.d.1935-03-07.5.1.62,1935-03-07,4430053b-1f47-481d-9354-7a7535f63be9,ca.m.8546,Sir GEORGE PERLEY:,Minister Without Portfolio,UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE,MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION,,I do not read

the subclause in that way at all. This is practically the same as the British act except that they require a period of ten instead of six weeks. But the way we have it is better. By the second statutory condition the receipt of benefits depends on continuous unemployment. Literally construed this would be a severe condition and would tend to discourage an unemployed person from seeking work for short periods or for the odd day. This tendency would not be for the benefit of the insurance fund or of insured persons. The rule in this subsection is that any three days of unemployment within a period of six days shall be treated as continuous and that any two such periods separated by not more than six weeks shall be treated as one. In the British acts, ""continuously unemployed"" has always been subject to statutory definition, and since 1923, the definition has been as above except that the ""'bridge"" between two periods has been changed. They changed this ""bridge"" several times in England. Prior to 1923 the ""bridge"" was six weeks. In that year it was made three weeks; in 1924, six weeks, and in 1927, against the recommendation of the Blanesburgh committee that no change should be made, the ""bridge"" was increased to ten weeks. The process of change and extension in the British scheme may have been to some extent associated with the exigencies of the circumstances leading to the increasing departure of that scheme from an insurance basis. The fact that the ""bridge was six weeks prior to 1923; that it was restored to six weeks in 1924, and that the Blanesburgh committee recommended in 1927 that it should remain at six weeks, is of more than passing significance. For that reason the six weeks' period has been adopted in our case.
